newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leading Bavarian denies EMU delay would boost mark.
newsitem.headline: Leading Bavarian denies EMU delay would boost mark.

text.p: A delay to Europe's proposed single currency would not result in a feared appreciation of the deutschemark, a leading figure in German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) said on Monday.
"There is no reason for the assumption that a delay of one year would lead to a threatening appreciation of the D-mark," said Bavaria's economics minister Otto Wiesheu.
Wiesheu's comments were the latest in a fierce debate in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.
Another leading figure in Waigel's party -- Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber -- has issued persistent hardline warnings against any relaxation of the criteria for the euro.
Stoiber's warnings about meeting strict fiscal criteria for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) have drawn strong rebukes from Kohl and leaders in his Christian Democrats (CDU).

Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) said on Monday the row could cause irreparable harm to Kohl's centre-right coalition, made up of his CDU, its Bavarian sister party the CSU and the FDP.
Wiesau said the FDP in particular had overplayed the danger to the mark of a delay to the euro.
"(They) have overlooked that the exchange rate has been at a stable level for some time," he said.

Wieshau said the current strength of the British and U.S. economies spoke against extreme currency fluctuations and said a delay to the start of EMU would not damage Germany's export sector by boosting the mark.

Wiesau restated his party's insistence on a stable euro. He said participants in EMU must fulfil the target of holding government deficits to within three percent of GDP at the launch of the euro or the project may be seen as uncredible.

"If the impression of financial policy laxity firmed on the international financial markets then the euro would tend towards weakness," he said. "This would have to be paid for with higher inflation rates and risk supplements."
